Found a price data quality issue (135 listings above $2,000/night, including test entries) still pending resolution. Identified that entire-home listings command the highest prices while smaller, unique formats (guesthouses, tiny homes, guest suites) show higher booking frequency relative to price, and that this niche's demand is concentrated in central/east neighborhoods. Ran a Kruskal-Wallis test (chi-squared = 17.8, p < 0.001) with Holm-corrected pairwise Wilcoxon comparisons confirming East Austin and Cherrywood have statistically higher booking frequency (reviews/month) than South Austin for this niche, while East Austin and Cherrywood do not differ from each other.

Looking at room type breakdown: entire homes dominate supply with the highest price and strong ratings, private rooms are cheaper but similarly well-rated, and hotel rooms stand out oddly with high prices but low ratings and near-zero review counts, suggesting weak demand or newer listings. I'm now turning to property type, using reviews per month as a demand proxy, and noticing tiny homes, guesthouses, and guest suites show the highest booking frequency.

I want to flag that this reviews-per-month metric is an imperfect demand signal since not everyone leaves reviews, and price isn't normalized for listing size, plus I excluded outliers above $2000. I'll wrap up with a concise summary of findings and some suggested follow-up questions.

Filtered out the 135 listings priced above $2,000/night (pending your outlier decision) to avoid them distorting these summaries.

**By room type**: Entire home/apt dominates the market (75% of listings after filtering) and commands the highest median price ($230/night), with strong ratings (4.93) and typical review counts. Private rooms are much cheaper (median $95) but earn comparably high ratings (4.95) — quality isn't the differentiator, format is. Hotel rooms are priced similarly to entire homes ($280) but have a *median of 0 reviews* and lower ratings (4.5) — they seem to underperform on Airbnb specifically, plausibly because they're competing with real hotel booking channels.

**By property type**, using `n_reviews_per_month` as a demand proxy (booking frequency, independent of how long a listing has been active) rather than raw review count:

| property type | n | median price | median reviews/mo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tiny home | 127 | $157 | 2.40 |
| Entire guesthouse | 516 | $160 | 2.03 |
| Entire guest suite | 183 | $143 | 1.81 |
| Entire bungalow | 99 | $240 | 1.47 |
| Entire home | 4,200 | $320 | 1.42 |
| Entire rental unit | 1,947 | $169 | 1.39 |
| Private room in home | 811 | $73 | 0.33 |
| Room in hotel | 491 | $294 | 0.42 |

The pattern worth noting: smaller, self-contained unit types — tiny homes, guesthouses, guest suites — book more frequently per month than the higher-priced "entire home" category, despite roughly half the nightly rate. That's a demand-per-listing signal, not a revenue signal; I haven't multiplied price × turnover to see which format actually earns more. Private rooms and hotel-style listings show comparatively weak booking frequency on this platform.

One caveat: `n_reviews_per_month` undercounts true bookings since not every guest leaves a review, and it doesn't account for `minimum_nights` (a listing with 30-night minimums will naturally show fewer, larger bookings). Also haven't looked at whether these property-type patterns hold consistently across neighborhoods, or vary a lot.

I used a Kruskal-Wallis test rather than ANOVA since the demand distribution (reviews/month) is right-skewed with a long tail of high-performing outliers in each neighborhood — the boxplot shows clearly non-normal shapes with unequal spread. I imputed `NA` values in `n_reviews_per_month` as 0 (12 of 411 listings), since these correspond to listings with no reviews yet (`first_review` also `NA`), i.e., genuinely no observed demand.

**Kruskal-Wallis**: $$\chi^2(2) = 17.8, p < 0.001$$ — there is a statistically detectable difference in demand across the three neighborhoods.

**Pairwise comparisons** (Wilcoxon rank-sum, Holm-corrected):

| Comparison | p-value |
|---|---|
| East Austin vs. South Austin | 0.0002 |
| Cherrywood vs. South Austin | 0.028 |
| East Austin vs. Cherrywood | 0.96 |

South Austin shows meaningfully lower booking frequency than both East Austin and Cherrywood, which are statistically indistinguishable from each other. This supports the earlier lead: for this guesthouse/tiny-home/guest-suite niche, East Austin and Cherrywood show genuinely higher demand than South Austin, not just noise from small samples.

Caveats worth keeping in mind: this is an observational comparison, not causal — it doesn't tell you *why* South Austin underperforms (could be oversupply, different sub-neighborhoods lumped together, price positioning, etc.), and reviews-per-month remains an imperfect demand proxy (affected by minimum-night stays and review propensity). I also haven't corrected for the fact that this was one of several comparisons you might make across this analysis (neighborhood × property type has many possible cells), so treat this as a targeted confirmatory check rather than a fishing expedition.
